entry: American retired boxer and television personality, the daughter of [[Muhammad Ali]]. She began boxing at age 18 and fought professionally from 1999 to 2007, retiring undefeated. Her titles included the WBC, WIBA, IWBF and IBA female super middleweight championships and the IWBF light heavyweight title. Her first professional bout, against April Fowler in October 1999, ended in a first-round knockout. She later hosted *Home Made Simple* on OWN, co-hosted *American Gladiators* and served as a fitness correspondent on CBS's *The Early Show*.

Economic system in which transactions between private individuals are free from interventionism, such as subsidies or regulations. The French phrase, meaning "let do," probably originated at a meeting around 1681 between Jean-Baptiste Colbert and French merchants, when M. Le Gendre replied "Laissez-nous faire." The Physiocrats advocated the principle and a tax on land rent alone. [[Adam Smith]]'s *The Wealth of Nations* (1776) popularized it, and laissez-faire capitalism emerged in the mid-18th century. Proponents argue for a near-complete separation of government from the economic sector. Critics contend that it permits unchecked concentrations of power and negative externalities such as pollution.

Lake on the border of [[Uganda]] and the [[Democratic Republic of the Congo]]. It is Africa's sixth-largest lake and the second largest of Uganda's Great Lakes. The northernmost lake of the Albertine Rift chain, it is about 160 km long and 30 km across at its widest, with a maximum depth of 51 m and a surface elevation of 619 m. Its main sources are the [[White Nile]], which comes from [[Lake Victoria]] to the southeast, and the Semliki River. The outlet at its northern tip is the Albert Nile section of the White Nile. The water stays relatively stable in temperature, typically around 27–29 °C. The lake has 55 fish species, and the Nile perch is its largest predator apart from Nile crocodiles. Fisheries supply as much as 30% of Uganda's fish production. Four of its six haplochromine cichlids are endemic.

Rift lake in southern [[Siberia]], [[Russia]], and the deepest lake in the world. With a maximum depth of 1,642 m, it is also the largest freshwater lake by volume, holding 23,615.39 km³ of water, or 22–23% of the world's fresh surface water, more than all of the [[Great Lakes|North American Great Lakes]] combined. Its surface area of 31,722 km² is slightly larger than [[Belgium]], making it the seventh-largest lake by area and the second-largest in [[Eurasia]] after the [[Caspian Sea]]. At an estimated 25–30 million years old, it is the oldest lake in the world. Its basin lies in a rift zone where the Earth's crust is slowly pulling apart. Lake Baikal holds thousands of species of plants and animals, many of them endemic. UNESCO declared it a [[World Heritage Site]] in 1996.

Lake in southeastern [[Kazakhstan]]. It is one of the largest lakes in Asia and the 15th largest in the world, covering about 16,400 km². The lake lies in an endorheic basin fed by seven rivers, chiefly the Ili, which carries most of the inflow from mountains in China's [[Xinjiang]] region. Its western part is fresh and its eastern half saline, and a narrow central strait divides the two. Like the [[Aral Sea]], Balkhash is shrinking because of water diversion and extraction from its feeders; it covered an estimated 23,464 km² in 1910 and 15,730 km² by 1946. The largest shore city, also named Balkhash, has about 66,000 inhabitants, and the local economy rests on mining, ore processing and fishing. The lake became part of Kazakhstan after the dissolution of the [[Soviet Union]] in 1991.

Endorheic freshwater lake at the junction of [[Nigeria]], [[Niger]], [[Chad]] and [[Cameroon]] in western and central Africa. Its catchment area exceeds 1,000,000 km², and it is one of Africa's important freshwater fish-producing areas. The main source of water is the Chari River. The lake's area changes dramatically with the seasons. Its open water shrank from 25,000 km² in 1960 to just 2,000 km² in 1980, owing to climate change and human water diversion. Rainfall has partly recovered, and the lake is no longer estimated to be shrinking, although it remains threatened by [[Climate change|climate change]]. During a wetter past the basin held Mega-Chad, which covered about 400,000 km² and flowed into the Benue River. Around 900 AD, the Kanem people unified nomadic tribes into the Kanem Empire northeast of the lake.

Mountainous region and national park in [[Cumbria]], northwestern England. Its fells include England's highest peaks: Scafell Pike (978 m), Helvellyn (950 m) and Skiddaw (931 m). The region has sixteen major lakes. Windermere, the longest and largest lake in England, is 18 km long, and Wast Water, at 79 m, is the deepest. The area has literary associations with Beatrix Potter, John Ruskin, Arthur Ransome and the Lake Poets, including [[William Wordsworth]]. The Lake District National Park, established on May 9, 1951, covers 2,362 km² and is the largest of the thirteen national parks in England and Wales. The park received 17.73 million tourist visitors in 2024. Its central area was designated a [[World Heritage Site]] in 2017 as a cultural landscape.

Southernmost, shallowest and smallest by volume of the five [[Great Lakes]] of North America. Lake Erie is the fourth-largest of the five by surface area and the eleventh-largest lake in the world, with an area of 26,000 km². It lies on the international boundary between Canada and the United States. Its northern shore is in [[Ontario]], and [[Michigan]], Ohio, Pennsylvania and New York border it to the west, south and east. The main outflow is the Niagara River, whose turbines produce hydroelectric power near [[Niagara Falls]]. The western basin averages only 7.6 to 9.1 m in depth, and the lake's deepest point, 64 m, lies above sea level, the only Great Lake with this feature. During the [[War of 1812]], a U.S. naval victory at the Battle of Lake Erie on September 10, 1813, secured control of the lake. Nutrient pollution, particularly [[Phosphorus|phosphorus]] from agricultural runoff, fuels recurrent harmful algal blooms.

One of the five [[Great Lakes]] of North America, shared by the Canadian province of [[Ontario]] and the U.S. state of [[Michigan]]. The name derives from early French explorers, who named it for the indigenous Huron (Wyandot) people of the region. Hydrologically, Lake Huron forms part of a single body with [[Lake Michigan]], to which it is joined by the Straits of Mackinac; the two share the same surface elevation. Its main inlet is the St. Marys River from [[Lake Superior]], and its outlet is the St. Clair River to [[Lake Erie]]. The second-largest Great Lake by surface area, it covers about 59,600 km² and has a maximum depth of 229 m. Water flows through it faster than through the other Great Lakes, with a retention time of only 22 years. Invasive zebra and quagga mussels have altered its ecology since the late 20th century.

Artificial reservoir on the [[Zambezi]] River, bordering [[Zambia]] and [[Zimbabwe]], and the world's largest artificial lake by volume. It was filled between 1958 and 1963 after completion of the [[Dam|Kariba Dam]] at its northeastern end, flooding the Kariba Gorge. The lake lies about 1,300 km upstream from the mouth of the Zambezi on the [[Indian Ocean]]. It is about 280 km long and up to 32 km wide, with a maximum depth of 120 m. The dam was built to generate hydroelectric power for Zambia and Zimbabwe, then Northern and Southern Rhodesia. Flooding displaced local Tonga communities, and Operation Noah relocated more than 6,000 animals to higher ground between 1958 and 1961. The inshore fishery produces about 25,000 to 30,000 tonnes a year (as of 2023), dominated by the [[Sardine|sardine]] *Limnothrissa miodon*, introduced in 1967–1969. As of 2025, drought had left usable storage at around 8%.

Freshwater lake in northwestern [[Russia]], near [[Saint Petersburg]], and the largest lake located entirely in Europe. It is comparable in size to [[Lake Ontario]] and covers about 17,700 km², making it the 14th-largest lake in the world by area and the second largest in Russia after [[Lake Baikal]]. It lies in the Republic of Karelia and Leningrad Oblast, is fed mainly by the Svir, Volkhov and Vuoksi rivers, and drains through the [[Neva]] into the Gulf of Finland. The lake has more than 650 islands, including the Valaam Archipelago, with monasteries dating to the 14th century. It is home to the Ladoga ringed seal, a freshwater subspecies. During the [[Siege of Leningrad]] in World War II, the frozen lake served as the "Road of Life," carrying supplies and evacuating civilians from 1941 to 1943.

African Great Lake in the southernmost part of the East African Rift system, between [[Malawi]], [[Mozambique]] and [[Tanzania]]. Also called Lake Nyasa, it is the fourth-largest freshwater lake in the world by volume and the ninth-largest by area, at about 29,500 km². It is the third-largest lake in Africa and the second deepest. The lake holds more fish species than any other lake in the world, including at least 700 species of [[Cichlid|cichlid]]. It is meromictic: its water layers do not mix, a condition maintained by chemical and thermal gradients. Mozambique declared its portion of the lake a reserve on June 10, 2011, while the Malawian part lies partly within Lake Malawi National Park.

Brackish lake in northwestern [[Venezuela]], connected to the Gulf of Venezuela by a narrow strait. Its hydrology may make it better classed as an [[Estuary|estuary]] or semi-enclosed bay, but it is commonly called a lake. Counted as a lake, it covers 13,512 km², which would make it the largest in South America, ahead of [[Lake Titicaca]]. It formed about 36 million years ago in the [[Andes]], making it one of the oldest lakes on Earth. The largest of its rivers is the Catatumbo. The fault in its northern section is rich in oil and gas, making the lake Venezuela's main oil-producing area. Eutrophication caused by oil pollution is a major environmental problem. About a quarter of the country's population lives around the lake, which has the most frequent [[Lightning|lightning]] on Earth, the Catatumbo lightning.

One of the five [[Great Lakes]] of North America and the only one lying entirely within the United States. It is shared by [[Wisconsin]], Illinois, Indiana and [[Michigan]], and ports along its shore include Chicago, Gary, Milwaukee and Green Bay. The lake is the second-largest of the Great Lakes by volume, at 1,180 cubic miles (4,900 km³), and by depth, which reaches 281 m; only [[Lake Superior]] is larger on both counts. At 57,757 km², it is the third-largest by surface area. Through the Straits of Mackinac it connects to [[Lake Huron]], with the same surface elevation, and the two are hydrologically a single lake. The name is believed to come from the [[Ojibwe]] word meaning "great water."

Freshwater lake on the border of [[Zambia]] and the [[Democratic Republic of the Congo]], lying on the longest arm of [[Congo River|the Congo]], Africa's second-longest river. It makes up 110 km of the river's length, between the Luapula River upstream and the Luvua River downstream. The lake covers about 5,120 km² and is shallow in the south, deepening to a maximum of 27 m in northern depressions. Its name means "lake" in several [[Bantu languages]], so it is often called simply Mweru. The fishery provides food, employment and income for around 400,000 people in the region. Deltas and swamps serve as breeding grounds for fish, and overexploitation has prompted co-management initiatives to protect fish stocks.

Freshwater lake in [[Nicaragua]], the largest in Central America. Of tectonic origin, it covers 8,264 km², making it the 19th-largest lake in the world by area and the tenth largest in the Americas. Its outflow is the San Juan River, which flows east to the [[Caribbean Sea]]. Bull sharks migrate into the lake from the Caribbean, and the volcanic island of Ometepe, the largest island in the lake, rises within it. Before the Panama Canal was built, a stagecoach line owned by [[Cornelius Vanderbilt]]'s company linked the lake with the Pacific, and a Nicaragua Canal was proposed. The United States secured canal rights in the Bryan–Chamorro Treaty of 1916, but the treaty was rescinded in 1970. In 2014 Nicaragua granted a 50-year concession for a canal at a cost of US$40 billion. Protests over its ecological and social effects, and doubts about financing, meant construction never began.

Freshwater lake in northwestern [[Russia]], the second-largest lake in Europe after [[Lake Ladoga]]. It covers about 9,700 km² and belongs to the [[Baltic Sea]] drainage basin. The lake is fed by about 50 rivers and drained by the Svir River, and it contains about 1,650 islands. Kizhi, one of them, hosts a historic complex of 89 Orthodox churches and other wooden structures dating from the 15th to 20th centuries. The complex, Kizhi Pogost, is a [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Site]]. About 1,200 petroglyphs (rock engravings), dated to the 4th–2nd millennia BC, are carved on the eastern shores, and they too are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The major cities on the lake are Petrozavodsk, Kondopoga and Medvezhyegorsk.

Easternmost and smallest by surface area of the five [[Great Lakes]] of North America. It forms part of the Canada–United States boundary, with its northern, western and southwestern shores in the Canadian province of [[Ontario]] and its southern and eastern shores in [[New York (state)|New York]]. Its primary inlet is the Niagara River from [[Lake Erie]]. As the last lake in the Great Lakes chain, it serves as the outlet to the Atlantic Ocean through the [[St. Lawrence River]], the western end of the [[St. Lawrence Seaway]]. The lake covers 18,960 km² and reaches a maximum depth of 244 m. Its surface is 75 m above sea level, the lowest of the Great Lakes. Major Canadian cities on its shore include [[Toronto]], Kingston, Mississauga, Hamilton and St. Catharines. The Long Sault control dam and the Moses-Saunders Power Dam regulate its water level.

Northernmost, westernmost and highest of the [[Great Lakes]] of North America, and the largest freshwater lake in the world by surface area. It straddles the Canada–United States border, with [[Ontario]] to the north and east and [[Minnesota]], [[Michigan]] and [[Wisconsin]] to the west and south. It holds about 12,100 km³ of water, making it the largest of the Great Lakes by volume and the third-largest freshwater lake in the world by volume. Its maximum depth is 406 m. The lake receives inflows from more than 200 rivers and drains into [[Lake Huron]] through the St. Marys River. Its cold, clear, low-nutrient water supports deepwater species adapted to minimal light.

Freshwater alpine lake in the [[Sierra Nevada]], straddling the border of [[California]] and [[Nevada]]. At 1,897 m above sea level, it is the largest alpine lake in North America. By volume it trails only the five [[Great Lakes]] among U.S. lakes. At 501 m deep, it is the second-deepest lake in the United States, after Crater Lake in Oregon. The lake is known for its clarity and mountain panorama. Winter sports and summer recreation draw visitors, and the Nevada side has several lakeside casino resorts.

African Great Lake in the western branch of the East African Rift, shared by [[Tanzania]], the [[Democratic Republic of the Congo]], [[Burundi]] and [[Zambia]]. It is the world's second-largest freshwater lake by volume and its second deepest, after [[Lake Baikal]], and it is also the longest freshwater lake in the world. Its maximum depth is 1,470 m. The lake drains via the Lukuga River into the [[Congo River]], which discharges into the [[Atlantic Ocean]] at Banana. Estimated to be 9 to 12 million years old, it is one of the oldest lakes on Earth. It supports more than 240 species of [[Cichlid|cichlid]] fishes, almost all found only in the basin.

Large lake in the [[Andes]] on the border of [[Peru]] and [[Bolivia]]. It is the largest lake in South America by surface area and volume. At 3,812 m above sea level, it is often called the highest navigable lake in the world. Although often listed as freshwater, its waters are slightly brackish. The lake covers about 8,372 km² and reaches a maximum depth of 281 m. Evaporation accounts for 95% of its outflow. The Uros people build floating islands from totora reeds. In [[Inca Empire|Inca]] mythology the lake is the birthplace of the sun god Inti, and it was a cradle of Andean civilizations, including the [[Tiwanaku]] culture. It was designated a Ramsar wetland of international importance in 1997.

Saline alkaline lake in the Kenyan Rift Valley, extending into Ethiopia at its far northern end. It is the world's largest permanent desert lake and largest alkaline lake. By volume it is the fourth-largest salt lake, after the [[Caspian Sea]], [[Issyk-Kul]] and [[Lake Van]]. Three rivers, the Omo, Turkwel and Kerio, flow into it, but with no outlet its only water loss is [[Evaporation|evaporation]]. The level fell 10 m between 1975 and 1993. The Omo supplies most of its water, and the Gilgel Gibe III Dam in Ethiopia threatens the lake. Its water is too saline and fluoride-rich for drinking. Lake Turkana National Parks are a [[World Heritage Site]], and the surrounding area has yielded abundant hominid fossils, including remains of [[Homo habilis]] and [[Homo erectus]].

Endorheic salt lake in northwestern [[Iran]], in the Iranian region of Azerbaijan near the [[Armenia|Armenian]] border. At its greatest extent it was the largest lake in [[West Asia]] and the sixth-largest saltwater lake on Earth, covering about 6,000 km² with a maximum depth of 20 m. Drought, dams on the rivers feeding it and groundwater pumping shrank it to 10% of its former size by late 2017. Water returned in 2019 after heavier rain and diversion from the Zab River, but drought and administrative mismanagement caused a renewed drop, and by September 2025 satellite imagery showed the lake almost dry. After heavy rainfall across the [[Fertile Crescent]] and releases from dams, its level rose in early 2026 to the highest in five years. The lake and its former islands are protected as a national park.

Largest lake in [[Turkey]], a saline soda lake in the Eastern Anatolia region, in the [[Armenia|Armenian]] highlands. It covers about 3,755 km² and reaches a maximum depth of 451 m. Its waters are highly alkaline, with a pH of 9.7 to 9.8. A volcanic eruption blocked its original outlet in prehistoric times, and it is one of the world's few endorheic lakes larger than 3,000 km². It holds 38% of Turkey's surface water, including rivers. At 1,640 m above sea level, the lake usually does not freeze because of its high salinity, although its shallow northern section sometimes does. The endemic pearl mullet lives in the lake, and the Van cat is noted for swimming in it.
